Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Reminders of victims' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type; it implies exposure to other victims in a disaster/assault context rather than illness-related trauma.

'Being naked' as a trigger is difficult to connect to life-threatening illness unless there is a very specific medical context; with the other selected items it appears context-incongruent rather than illness-linked.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Rehearsing conversations before any interaction suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety, but there are no corresponding appraisal or threat items about humiliation, criticism, or social danger; this strategy is poorly matched to the rest of the profile.

'Being naked' is a poor fit as a primary trigger for a life-threatening illness profile unless the illness/trauma specifically involved exposure or bodily vulnerability in that context; with the rest of this profile centered on somatic and medical cues, this item stands out as clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Rehearsing conversations before any interaction suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety or interpersonal threat management, which is not supported by the other selected trigger, memory, appraisal, or threat items and does not fit the stated illness-centered formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: Always choosing a safe/protected seat implies environmental danger monitoring more typical of assault/combat/public threat trauma than life-threatening illness; it is weakly connected to the medical/somatic trigger pattern here.

issues.item: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
issues.explanation: For a 37-year-old man with trauma centered on a life-threatening illness, the threat profile is otherwise strongly somatic/medical (negative emotions, body on alert) and the trigger/strategy pattern is specifically tied to breathlessness, procedures, and medical cues. A prominent exaggerated startle to ordinary sounds is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-related trigger network and from the cognitive formulation, where Threat is mainly linked with Maladaptive Strategies rather than a broad sensory hypervigilance pattern. This makes the item clinically incoherent relative to the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Marcus was thirty-seven when the shortness of breath started. He remembers the date exactly-March 14th, a Tuesday-because it was the morning after his daughter's school recital, an event he'd nearly skipped. He was sitting at his desk in the climate-controlled server room of his firm, staring at lines of code that suddenly seemed to swim before his eyes. His chest tightened. He couldn't draw a full breath. Within hours, the emergency room confirmed what the radiologist's voice on the phone would later make official: Stage III non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. The disease had been growing in his chest cavity for months, pressing against his lungs and heart, and he'd felt nothing until the moment his body simply refused to work properly.

What followed was eighteen months of chemotherapy, radiation, and the specific terror of watching his own mortality become a series of medical appointments. The treatments were brutal. He remembers the oncology suite-the smell of disinfectant and something chemical he couldn't name, the nurse's practiced efficiency as she inserted the central line into his chest, the cold sensation of the needle breaking skin, the way the IV bag dripped poison into his body with the promise that it might save his life. He remembers the CT scanner, the MRI machine, the PET scan, each one a moment of being enclosed in a tube while machines measured whether he was dying faster or slower than before. The breathlessness returned with every scan, not from the disease anymore but from panic-the feeling that he was trapped, that his body was betraying him again, that something unseen was growing inside him that the machines would find. His thoughts during those scans were intrusive and uncontrollable: images of the tumor returning, fragments of conversations with his oncologist replaying without warning, the certainty that any scan would reveal the cancer had come back and this time he wouldn't survive it.

He survived. The cancer went into remission. But the man who emerged from treatment was not the same. Now, five years later at forty-two, Marcus still cannot pass a hospital without his heart rate spiking. The sight of a needle-even in a television commercial, even held by a nurse on a billboard advertisement-triggers a cascade of physical sensation: his shoulders tense, his breathing becomes shallow, and a hot surge of something between fear and anger floods through him. He is certain that his body is still dangerous to him, that the cancer is waiting somewhere in his cells, and that any medical procedure-even a routine blood draw-is the beginning of the end. His sleep has become fragmented; he wakes at three in the morning with his heart pounding, sometimes without knowing why, other times because he has dreamed of the oncology suite or the scanner's mechanical voice telling him to hold still.

He has come to control what he can. His eating has become a careful mathematics: he weighs his portions, counts his calories, monitors his macronutrients with the precision he once applied to database architecture. The control is soothing. When he eats, he eats exactly what he has planned. When he doesn't eat, that too is planned. He has lost fifteen pounds in the past year. His ex-wife mentioned it during a custody exchange. He said nothing. Exercise is another thing he no longer does. The gym used to be his refuge, but now the exertion triggers the breathlessness, and the breathlessness brings back the panic from the scanner, from the IV line, from the moment in the oncology suite when he understood that his body had turned against him. It is easier not to go. His clothes fit differently now. His back hurts from sitting at his desk all day, but he does not address this because addressing it means seeing a doctor, and seeing a doctor means hospitals, needles, the cold certainty that something is wrong inside him that needs to be found.

He has not had a physical examination in five years. His primary care physician's office calls every six months. He does not return the calls. The thought of sitting in that waiting room, of a nurse taking his blood pressure, of a doctor listening to his chest with a stethoscope and asking him to breathe deeply-the very request to breathe deeply is a trigger now-fills him with a dread so complete that avoidance feels like the only rational choice. The consequences have accumulated quietly. His work performance has declined; concentration is harder when sleep is fragmented and anxiety is constant. He has missed his daughter's last two soccer seasons because the fields are near the hospital, and the proximity alone is enough to send him into a state of hypervigilance where he cannot focus on anything but the building's location in his peripheral vision. It is his daughter who finally brought him here. She is twelve now, old enough to notice that her father flinches at ambulance sirens, that he has stopped coming to her soccer games, that he seems always slightly afraid. She asked him, directly, if he was okay. He realized he could not answer honestly. He came to therapy because he could not bear for her to inherit his fear. What he hopes for most is to be able to breathe again without panic. What he fears most is that he will not.
